title: Your own experiment
hook: try a practice for a month and track how you feel

segments.voice: Yesterday: what can't be measured, and Pascal's heart with its reasons. Your line was beyond measure. What did you notice that no number would catch? Day one thousand three hundred fifty.

A printer in Philadelphia buys a small notebook. On each page he writes the name of one virtue he wants to grow into, and rules the page into a grid of days. Every evening he looks back and marks a small black spot wherever he fell short. The printer is Benjamin Franklin, and he tells this story himself in his autobiography. He's running an experiment, with one subject: himself. Today, after weeks of other people's studies, the lab is yours.
screen: `A PRINTER'S SMALL NOTEBOOK.` → `ONE VIRTUE PER PAGE.` → `A BLACK SPOT FOR EACH SLIP.`

segments.voice: First, Franklin's method. In his words: "I made a little book, in which I allotted a page for each of the virtues." He gave his attention to one virtue at a time and kept score honestly, spots and all. He admits the book filled with more faults than he'd expected. Second, why a personal experiment is worth doing. Studies tell us what tends to happen across many people. They can't tell you what a practice does in your life, with your schedule and your temperament. A month of careful trying can. Third, the honest limits. An experiment of one has no comparison group. Hopes shape what we notice; if you expect a practice to help, you may rate your days a little kinder. Life also moves on its own: a hard week at work can swamp any practice. So keep it simple. Pick one practice. Decide before you start what you'll track, maybe a one-to-five rating of your mood or sleep each night. Write it down at the same time every day. At the end, look at the whole month, not just the best day or the worst. Fourth, what you're really testing. Not whether a practice is true. Whether it helps you, here, now, and what it costs you. Franklin didn't become perfect. He said the attempt made him better and happier than he otherwise would have been. That's a modest finding. It's also the kind a person can actually use. My experiment.
screen: `A LITTLE BOOK, A PAGE PER VIRTUE.` · `STUDIES CAN'T TEST YOUR LIFE.` · `NO CONTROL GROUP; HOPES COLOR IT.` · then, large: `ONE PRACTICE, ONE MEASURE, ONE MONTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: start one month-long test. Sit comfortably and breathe. Let one practice from this path come forward, the one you're most curious about. Two hours outside. The slow breath. A mental photograph of a good moment. Coaching yourself by name. Choose just one. Then choose your measure: one number each night, one to five, for mood, sleep or calm. Picture the little notebook, or the note on your phone, where it will live. If you pray, you can offer the month as an intention. The bell holds the time.
Your own experiment. One practice, one simple measure, one month, read honestly, knowing hopes can color the results. Today's word.
Your line: my experiment. Today, write the first entry: the practice, the measure and tonight's number. Day one thousand three hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Some people test a practice on themselves for a month, choosing one simple daily rating before they start and reading the whole month at the end, much as Benjamin Franklin kept a little book of his virtues.

what it means: one practice, one measure chosen in advance, one month, read as a whole.
what a scholar hears: an n-of-1 trial, with no control and real expectation effects; useful for personal decisions, not for general claims.
